project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.
1 piece(s) of input or evidence text read like instructions to the AI and were replaced before the agents saw them (see the execution trace).

constraints: The lignin is currently routed to internal fuel, so diversion to a commercial product would require changing that use.
There is no lignin dryer, so buyers requiring dry powder would need to provide or install drying capacity.
Solvent or membrane fractionation is not available, limiting uses that require fractionated lignin unless additional processing is arranged.
Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting uses that require modified lignin unless additional processing is arranged.
The stream leaves the mill as wet cake, so moisture increases shipped mass and handling requirements.
The covered cake storage capacity is limited to 1500.0 t wet, constraining inventory buffering.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional_demo; the mill and stream are invented, and all values are illustrative assumptions rather than measurements.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing and require measurement before pathway or buyer specifications can be assessed.
The lignin-content analytical method is unclear and should be confirmed before comparisons with specifications.
Moisture is uncertain and should be verified through routine sampling because it determines dry tonnage and shipped mass.
The recorded production and composition ranges are assumed annual variability ranges, not demonstrated operating data.
agent.summary: Validated fictional profile: 40000.0 t/yr wet kraft lignin cake at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003, corresponding to 26000.0 t/yr dry mass; the balance and composition checks pass, but key characterization data and real mill measurements are absent.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for wood-based-panel adhesives, with typical replacement up to 50% after activation or depolymerization.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is supported for veneer plywood; UPM reports industrial proof and EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 performance.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include plywood producers and other wood-based-panel adhesive users.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin.
A plywood adhesive qualification cited for LPF resin is EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3; formaldehyde emissions were measured under EN 717-2.
One laboratory study evaluated viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard.

limitations: The strongest commercial-performance evidence is vendor technical literature and does not cite an independent test report.
The reported TRL 8 applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft-lignin resin.
The studies and replacement levels do not establish performance for Pinecrest's wet cake or unmodified lignin.
The cited laboratory plywood study used poplar samples and reports inconsistent standard identifiers.
missing_information: No lignin purchase price, resin-grade price, market volume available to Pinecrest, named buyers, contract terms, or regional demand is provided.
No evidence establishes whether Pinecrest's wet cake can meet resin-process moisture, ash, molecular-weight, or hydroxyl specifications.
No evidence quantifies drying, activation, depolymerization, logistics, or customer qualification costs.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents industrially proven LPF resin and a plywood qualification, but it does not document commercial sales by several producers or named established buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been tested as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane and polyisocyanurate foams.
Unmodified kraft lignin has also been studied in flexible polyurethane foam; the evidence suggests denser, stiffer foams may be suited to heavy-duty applications.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid insulation-foam producers and flexible-foam producers, including manufacturers serving heavy-duty foam applications.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: A cited acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups; this is not a phenolic-hydroxyl requirement.
Rigid PUR/PIR foam qualification was assessed against ASTM C1029-15 Type 1 specifications.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies rather than commercial production.
The studies cover multiple lignin types and do not establish a Pinecrest-specific kraft-lignin pass rate.
The evidence reports technical drawbacks including reduced compressive strength, altered density or stiffness, darker color, and possible sulfur odor.
The review evidence rates polyurethane uses at TRL 6 overall, not kraft-lignin foam specifically; another review says commercialization remains limited.
missing_information: No lignin price, polyol-replacement contract price, market volume, named buyers, or regional demand is provided.
Pinecrest's missing total hydroxyl, molecular-weight, composition, and sodium data prevent direct compatibility assessment.
No evidence quantifies the drying, modification, fractionation, or co-solvent equipment required for Pinecrest's wet cake.
No commercial customer qualification pathway, production trial, or contract terms are documented.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research testing and a broader TRL assessment, but it does not document a commercial lignin-foam sale, established buyer, or development partnership.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.

applications.statement: Lignin is supported as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the cited work found that its lignin-based fiber mechanical properties were about 50% of the target.

Kraft lignin is supported as a feedstock for hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; carbonized kraft lignin showed higher initial coulombic efficiency than sulfonated lignin in the cited comparison.
Lignin can be converted into activated carbon, including when the precursor is too impure for other uses, and lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include carbon-fiber precursor and carbon-fiber manufacturers.
Potential customers include sodium-ion battery anode-material developers and battery manufacturers.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is an incumbent or competing material for carbon fiber.
Anthracite and pitch are identified as fossil hard-carbon precursors competing with lignin for sodium-ion battery hard carbon.

qualification_requirements.statement: For carbon-fiber precursor use, cited ORNL specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber needed purification, and softwood lignin needs a plasticizing agent for melt spinning.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation, although lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.
Battery-material qualification can take 3 years according to Stora Enso's statement about qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers.

limitations: Carbon fiber, hard carbon, and activated carbon have substantially different requirements; evidence for one does not transfer to the others.
The carbon-fiber precursor study used lignin from a near-neutral hemicellulose extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping.
The carbon-fiber cost and performance evidence includes old targets, modelled costs, and a project summary rather than independently verified commercial results.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review, and the activated-carbon evidence is laboratory work using zinc chloride activation.
The battery qualification and pilot evidence comes from company investor material with forward-looking statements, and later status was not verified.
missing_information: No Pinecrest-specific ash, volatiles, residual carbohydrate, particulate, carbon yield, molecular-weight, or electrochemical performance data is provided.
No product price, volume demand, named buyers for Pinecrest, contract terms, or regional market size is provided.
No evidence determines whether Pinecrest's wet cake can be economically dried, purified, carbonized, activated, or otherwise processed for each carbon product.
No evidence establishes current operating status of the cited battery pilot or a confirmed customer qualification outcome.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents validated industrially relevant precursor development, a pilot production line announcement, and battery-manufacturer qualification activity, but it does not document several producers selling lignin-derived carbon materials to established buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin would need activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
Pinecrest would need chemical-modification capacity from a new installation or partner because the mill does not have that equipment.
A drying solution would be needed for buyers or processes requiring dry powder because the stream leaves as wet cake and the mill has no lignin dryer.
The project would need to manage diversion from internal fuel and covered wet-cake storage limited to 1500.0 t wet.
The cited plywood application would require qualification for EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde emissions measured under EN 717-2.

technical_maturity.statement: The pathway has a cited TRL of 8, mapped by the readiness assessment to a technical-readiness score of 5.

adoption_barriers.statement: Customers would need to qualify the lignin-containing resin against phenol-based resin performance and application requirements.
Pinecrest-specific resin-grade moisture, ash, molecular-weight, and hydroxyl suitability has not been established.
No named buyers, purchase terms, regional demand, or customer qualification costs are documented.

decision.ranking_source: score_and_rank, called by the Decision Agent

main_drivers: It is the only pathway meeting the engine’s minimum assessed-weight threshold, with 0.8 of criterion weight assessed; its attractiveness is 2.19 with a range of 1.95–2.75.
Technical readiness is 3, based on TRL 5, and market evidence is 3, supported by validated precursor development, a pilot-line announcement, and battery-manufacturer qualification activity.

Feedstock compatibility is the main negative driver: it scores 1 because the checked carbon-fiber requirements show a largest relative gap of 900%; commercialization feasibility scores 2 because drying, purification, carbonization or activation, and qualification assets or partners are not yet identified.

Indicative economics is unassessed because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing; evidence quality is high to moderate across four cited records. The compatibility result applies to carbon-fiber precursor and may not represent other carbon products.
what_could_change_it: Pinecrest-specific testing showing acceptable ash, volatiles, residual carbohydrate, particulate content, carbon yield, and product performance—especially for activated carbon rather than carbon fiber—could improve feedstock compatibility and feasibility.
A sourced product price, realistic yield, and variable-cost model could materially increase or decrease the pathway’s attractiveness by filling the unassessed economics criterion.

A confirmed operating pilot, customer qualification result, or purchase commitment could improve market evidence and commercialization feasibility; evidence that the cited pilot is inactive could weaken them.
A drying, purification, carbonization, or activation partner offering a defined tolling price and capacity could improve feasibility; high delivered processing or logistics costs could reduce it.

main_drivers: The engine reports attractiveness of 3.73 with a range of 2.5–4.3, but it is insufficient-data because only 0.55 of criterion weight is assessed; feedstock compatibility and indicative economics are unassessed.
It has the strongest technical-readiness result, scoring 5 from TRL 8, while market evidence scores 3 and commercialization feasibility scores 3.

Its position is supported by industrially proven LPF resin and a plywood qualification, but Pinecrest lacks drying and chemical-modification capability and would need a processing or activation/depolymerization partner and customer qualification.
Evidence quality is high to moderate across two cited records. The apparently higher attractiveness is not a completed ranking because the minimum completeness threshold was not met.
what_could_change_it: Measured Pinecrest moisture, ash, molecular-weight, and hydroxyl data against a resin-process specification could assess the currently missing feedstock-compatibility criterion.
A pilot with a resin producer or plywood customer, followed by qualification results or a purchase commitment, could improve market evidence and feasibility; failed qualification could lower them.

A sourced resin-grade or treated-lignin price, product yield, and variable-cost estimate—including drying, activation or depolymerization, and logistics—could establish indicative economics and either promote or weaken the pathway.
Evidence that Pinecrest can sell wet cake into a compatible process, or alternatively quantified drying requirements and costs, could materially change feasibility.

main_drivers: The engine reports attractiveness of 2.36 with a range of 1.75–3.55, but it is insufficient-data because only 0.55 of criterion weight is assessed; feedstock compatibility and indicative economics are unassessed.

Technical readiness scores 3 from TRL 6, market evidence scores 2, and commercialization feasibility scores 2. The market score reflects research testing without a documented commercial lignin-foam sale, established buyer, or development partnership.
The pathway is constrained by missing total-hydroxyl, molecular-weight, composition, and sodium data, plus the absence of drying, modification, fractionation, and customer-qualification capability.
Evidence quality is high to moderate across three cited records. The higher end of its range reflects unresolved evidence gaps, not demonstrated performance.
what_could_change_it: Measured total hydroxyl value, molecular weight, composition, sodium, and treatment response could establish feedstock compatibility and identify a viable modification route.

A production trial with a polyurethane producer demonstrating foam or polyol performance, followed by customer qualification or a development partnership, could improve market evidence and feasibility; unsuccessful trials could lower them.

A sourced polyol-replacement price, product yield, and variable-cost model—including drying, oxypropylation, depolymerization or liquefaction, co-solvent, and logistics costs—could establish economics and change the pathway’s position.
A partner with suitable modification and drying assets could improve feasibility; evidence that the required chemistry is incompatible with Pinecrest lignin could reduce it.

validation_steps.action: Characterize the wet cake and produce a dry, representative sample: measure moisture, ash, molecular weight, phenolic and total hydroxyl values, sodium, volatiles, residual carbohydrate, and particulate content.
validation_steps.reason: This fills the principal feedstock gaps and determines whether the material can meet pathway-specific requirements rather than relying on generic lignin assumptions.

validation_steps.action: Run small-scale application trials with one qualified partner in each pathway, using the actual Pinecrest material and documenting pretreatment, yield, and product performance.
validation_steps.reason: Direct trials can distinguish resin, polyurethane, activated-carbon, and carbon-fiber opportunities and generate customer-relevant qualification evidence.

validation_steps.action: Obtain written commercial offers or term sheets from processors and potential buyers for drying, modification, fractionation, carbonization or activation, and the resulting products.
validation_steps.reason: Partner capacity, delivered prices, customer specifications, and qualification requirements are currently unresolved.

validation_steps.action: Build a pathway-specific mass balance and contribution model using measured yield, sourced product price, variable costs, drying and logistics costs, and any toll-processing charges.
validation_steps.reason: Indicative economics is unassessed for every pathway because yield, price, and variable costs are missing; this step makes the economic comparison possible.

ranking_changers: A completed phenolic-resin economics and compatibility assessment could move phenolic resins into the ranked set and potentially above carbon materials, given its technical-readiness score of 5 and feasibility score of 3.

Carbon-material testing that demonstrates an economically viable non-carbon-fiber product could remove the current compatibility penalty; conversely, confirmation that Pinecrest cannot meet the selected product’s specifications would weaken the current rank.
A commercial polyurethane trial or buyer commitment could raise its market and feasibility assessment, while failed hydroxyl-response or customer trials could lower it.
Delivered economics—especially product yield, price, drying, downstream processing, and logistics—could change the ordering once the currently unassessed economics criterion is scored.
caveats: The Pinecrest feedstock and dashboard assessment are fictional, as specified.

The engine ranked only carbon materials because it assessed 0.8 of criterion weight for that pathway; phenolic resins and polyurethanes each had 0.55 assessed and were therefore reported as insufficient data, not as poor pathways.
Attractiveness values and ranges for insufficient-data pathways are not completed rankings. Missing evidence should not be interpreted as a low score.
Product output, revenue, gross contribution, and contribution per tonne were not calculated because product yield, product price, and variable costs were unavailable.

The carbon-material feedstock score is based on checked carbon-fiber precursor requirements; it does not establish compatibility with every carbon-material product. The current fuel use, wet-cake form, limited covered storage, absent dryer, and absent modification or fractionation equipment remain practical constraints.
report.summary: The deterministic engine places carbon materials first, but only provisionally: it is the sole pathway with enough assessed weight to rank, and its score is held back by poor checked carbon-fiber compatibility, missing economics, and substantial downstream capability needs. Phenolic resins appear most promising on technical maturity and have the highest uncompleted attractiveness, but they require feedstock and economic validation before a formal ranking. Polyurethanes trail on maturity, market evidence, and feasibility, with especially important hydroxyl and modification uncertainties. The next decision should be based on representative feedstock characterization, partner trials, written processing and buyer offers, and pathway-specific economics.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
